design:
Decisions, each with its why. HOW is left to the build except where a decision fixes a contract.

- D1 — One event, one refresh per resource. A tab handles each stream event once, however many panels show the affected data. Why: the subscriber count, not the event count, is the multiplier.
- D2 — Coalesce rather than cancel. A refresh asked for while the same request is in flight becomes at most one follow-up request, sent when the first answers. Why: a client-side cancel does not stop the Hub serving the request.
- D3 — Apply what the event already carries without a request. That covers an output line, a context-usage reading, and the fields of a run or queue change. Why: refetching the full history on every line is the largest bytes cost, and it grows with the conversation.
- D4 — Polls are backstops, not the freshness mechanism. Anything the stream already reports is polled at most every 30s. Why: the 3s and 5s polls make up most of the idle traffic.
- D5 — A list route's cost does not depend on how much history the project has. Each agent's and conversation's newest context-usage reading and newest output are found without reading the older ones. Why: these are the costs that grow 10-20x at 10x history.
- D6 — A request computes shared facts once. Roster availability and provider holds are computed once per `/loops` and `/jobs` request, not once per loop and check.
- D7 — An event stream holds no database connection while it streams. Authentication finishes its database work before streaming starts.
- D8 — Runner-agnostic (operator, 2026-10-25). Nothing in this slice may depend on which runner produced an event. The run-budget drive streams a real turn on Claude (Haiku) and on Copilot, the operator's two runners now. The Codex path is covered by replaying a recorded Codex event stream through the Hub until the operator's Codex account exists; then it is driven live.
- D9 — Every criterion is checked by one scenario of the slice's drive. The drive is `scripts/drive/perf_responsive.py`, and each criterion's `how_to_check` names its scenario (`--scenario <name>`). An agent runs them unaided; the browser scenarios use a headless page with a request log.
- Budgets are provisional (operator, 2026-10-25). The numbers stand as set until the operator has used the build on the work VDI, then they are tightened or loosened.
- Hazard (Tier 2 by CLAUDE.md):
  - The index is a migration that runs on the operator's real database at their next `:8000` restart. It is additive only; rollback drops it.
  - A committed UI bundle reaches the operator's live app on their next reload, so the bundle ships only with the slice's drive green.

problem:
Measured on the operator's Hub and on a copy of its database (roadmap `agentweave-performance-overhaul`; reports in `C:\Users\huida\aw-perf\`).

1. The dashboard multiplies each live event.
   - Each of about 20 stream subscribers on the chat screen re-runs the full invalidation switch (`hub/ui/src/hooks/useSSE.ts:415-455`, `:458-690`, added at `:696`).
   - A new request for a key cancels the one in flight. Nothing reaches the Hub, because no fetch carries an abort signal (`hub/ui/src/api/client.ts:10-20`), so the Hub serves both.
   - An agent-list refresh also refetches each agent's last 200 output lines, about 250KB, which are then discarded (`hub/ui/src/api/agents.ts:554,567`).
   - Each output line refetches the conversation's full history: 1.28MB for a 764-line conversation (`hub/ui/src/api/agentChat.ts:360`).
   - That is an estimated 1,300 requests per run, about 350 a minute.
   - Idle, it is about 52 a minute, from 3-second polls of questions and permission requests and a 5-second output poll that never stops.
2. Hot routes do work that grows with history.
   - `/agents` (`hub/hub/api/v1/agents.py:418-433`) and both conversation lists (`hub/hub/api/v1/agent_chat.py:400-438`) load every context-usage reading ever recorded. That is 3,034 rows, 61% of `event_logs`, only to use the newest.
   - At 10x history `/agents` costs 1.8s alone.
   - `/loops` issues 220 SQL statements for 3 loops, because availability and holds are recomputed per loop and per check (`hub/hub/api/v1/jobs.py:506`, `hub/hub/scheduler.py:1201,1358,1411,1849`, `hub/hub/provider_allowance.py:129-157`).
   - The latest-output-per-agent reads scan every output row (`agents.py:437-455`, `agent_activity.py:101`): 19.5ms, against 1.9ms with an index.
3. Event streams hold the database.
   - Every open event stream holds a database connection until it disconnects (`hub/hub/auth.py:177,233`).
   - With a pool of 5 plus 10 overflow, the 16th open stream fails with 500, and every read then waits 30s.
   - Two windows with several tabs and reconnects reach that.

The Hub serves requests on one event loop, so this volume queues even where each request is cheap. In production `/accounting`, which costs 6ms alone, took 1.8s. The events that drive the storm are emitted the same way whichever runner streams the turn. Claude, Copilot and Codex output all go through one recording function and one broadcast.

requirements.rationale: About 20 subscribers each re-run the whole invalidation today, so one context_warning costs about 44 requests on the chat screen.
requirements.statement: For any single stream event, an open dashboard tab sends at most one request per distinct resource the event affects, however many panels on screen show that resource.

requirements.rationale: A client-side cancel does not stop the Hub serving the cancelled request, so cancelling and resending doubles the Hub's work.
requirements.statement: A dashboard tab never has two identical GET requests to the Hub in flight at the same time. A refresh asked for while one is in flight results in at most one further request, sent after the first answers.

requirements.rationale: Today each output line refetches the full conversation (1.28MB for 764 lines). Each agent-list refresh refetches 200 output lines per agent, only to discard them.
requirements.statement: An agent output line or context-usage reading delivered on the stream appears on screen without the tab re-requesting the conversation's history, an agent's recent output, or the agent list.

requirements.rationale: Estimated today: about 350 a minute during a run and 52 a minute idle. The budget bounds the queue a weak CPU must drain. The numbers are provisional until the operator has tried the build on the work VDI.
requirements.statement: With the chat screen open on a conversation whose agent is streaming a turn, on any runner, a dashboard tab sends no more than 40 requests to the Hub in any minute. With nothing running and the app idle, it sends no more than 6 a minute.

requirements.rationale: Measured today: 80-93ms, 49-138ms and 40-107ms, growing at 10x to 1,784ms, 960ms and 962ms. Almost all of that is decoding every context reading.
requirements.statement: GET /agents, GET /conversations and GET /agent/{agent}/conversations each answer in under 60ms on a copy of the operator's database. On a copy with ten times its agent_outputs, event_logs and trace_spans, each answers in under 1.5 times its time on the original copy.

requirements.rationale: Measured today: 220 statements and 192-410ms, because availability and holds are recomputed per loop and per check.
requirements.statement: GET /loops and GET /jobs each issue no more than 25 SQL statements and answer in under 80ms on a copy of the operator's database (3 loops, 5 agents).

requirements.rationale: This slice changes cost only. A cheaper route that answers differently is a behaviour change nobody asked for.
requirements.statement: For the same database state, GET /agents, GET /conversations, GET /agent/{agent}/conversations, GET /loops and GET /jobs return the same response bodies after this change as before it.

requirements.rationale: Measured today: each open stream holds a pooled database connection. The 16th stream fails with 500, and reads then wait 30s.
requirements.statement: With 50 event streams open against one Hub, opening another stream succeeds, and GET /agents answers in under 1 second.

requirements.rationale: Measured today: the same burst takes 2.16s wall, the sum of the solo costs, because the loop serves them one after another.
requirements.statement: On a copy of the operator's database, a burst of 24 concurrent requests made of the dashboard's poll mix (agents, loops, conversations, an agent's output, accounting, an agent's conversations, tasks, questions) completes with every request answered within 600ms.

in_scope: How the dashboard reacts to stream events: which requests it sends, how many, and whether event payloads are applied in place
Dashboard polling intervals for data the stream already reports
Server cost of /agents, /conversations, /agent/{agent}/conversations, /loops, /jobs and the latest-output reads behind /agents and /tasks
Database connection use by the two event-stream routes
An additive index on agent_outputs for the latest-output reads
The run-budget behaviour on every runner: Claude, Copilot and Codex
non_goals: Changing what any screen shows: counts, statuses, context readings and output must read the same as today
Git or other blocking work on the event loop (slice turns-and-approvals-never-freeze)
Journal mode, retention and vacuum (slice database-stays-fast-as-history-grows)
Bundle splitting, timeline virtualization and first-open request count (slice opens-fast-on-a-weak-machine)
Paginating chat history or the task list (slice opens-fast-on-a-weak-machine)
Wiring abort signals into fetches: that saves bytes, not Hub work

summary: While an agent streams a turn on any runner, the dashboard asks the Hub for each changed thing once instead of tens of times. The hot list routes stop scaling with history, and open event streams stop holding database connections. Together these remove the request storm that makes ordinary reads take 1.6-3.6s, and up to 27s, on the operator's Hub.
